Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 and, where applicable, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956: custody/guardianship analysis is statute- and fact-specific, with the child's welfare a paramount consideration.

Other personal laws and special statutes (for example, those governing Muslim, Christian or Parsi families) may differ. The applicable law depends on the parties' personal law and the proceedings chosen.
Family Courts Act, 1984: establishment and jurisdiction of Family Courts, where notified for the area.
Identify the governing personal law and the forums available.
Choose the proceeding or combination; coordinate so that orders do not conflict and so that amounts awarded under one are accounted for in another.
Prepare a clear statement of income, expenses and the child's needs: schooling, health, care.
Seek interim maintenance and interim arrangements for the child. Ask for a disclosure affidavit from the other parent.
Propose a workable access schedule and explore mediation, which many family courts encourage.
If non-payment follows an order, consider enforcement steps available under the relevant statute.

docs.x: Marriage and birth certificates; income proofs and bank statements; evidence of the child's schooling and medical care; evidence of caregiving; earlier orders; communications about access; any police or protection complaints.

forum.x: Family Court or District Court as applicable; Magistrate for maintenance under the criminal procedure provision; High Court for revision or appeal.

items: Interim orders are commonly made on the available material; the amount depends on proof of the Respondent's means and the child's needs.
Custody and access are decided on the child's welfare; continuity of care and the child's wishes (where appropriate for age) are considered.
Parallel proceedings can lead to adjustment of amounts to avoid double recovery.

lessons.x: "Custody always goes to the mother." The welfare principle governs, not a rule favouring either parent. "I can ignore a maintenance order if I disagree." Non-compliance has legal consequences. Keep records of care and expenses.

faq: Can I file under more than one law?
Often yes, but courts may adjust amounts to avoid overlap, so coordination matters.

notcovered.x: International relocation, foreign custody orders, adoption.

sources.x: BNSS 2023; Hindu Marriage Act 1955; HAMA 1956; DV Act 2005; Guardians and Wards Act 1890; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956; Family Courts Act 1984; official repository for authority on disclosure and overlap.

scenarios.title: Minority Shareholder Oppression
scenarios.meta_title: Minority Shareholder Oppression | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on oppression and mismanagement of a minority shareholder in an Indian private company: evidence, NCLT remedies and information...
scenarios.question: What can a minority shareholder do if excluded from management and benefits of a closely held company?

facts.x: A fictional minority shareholder holds a modest stake in a fictional family-run private company and was a director until removed at a general meeting held on short notice. No dividends have been declared for years. Family members of the majority shareholder draw salaries and the company has made loans and a property transfer to related parties. The minority shareholder has not received accounts for two years and was not invited to later meetings.

problem.x: The minority shareholder wants information, a fair exit or a restoration of rights, and needs to know whether the company's conduct meets the legal standard.

items: Whether the conduct is oppressive or mismanagement and not merely a majority decision the minority dislikes.
Eligibility to apply.
Evidence of related-party transactions and diversion.
Interim relief.
Available remedies.
Limitation and delay.

Companies Act, 2013, Sections 241 and 242: relief for oppression and mismanagement and the Tribunal's powers (regulating conduct, buy-out, restricting transactions, setting aside agreements, interim orders).
Section 244: eligibility thresholds for members to apply and the Tribunal's power to waive them.

Companies Act provisions on meeting notice, annual general meetings, financial statements, statutory registers, member inspection rights and related-party transactions must be identified by section and checked against the company's articles and applicable rules.

Removal of a director is governed by Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013, subject to statutory exceptions and the special-notice and hearing requirements. Confirm the director's category, the company's constitution and the exact procedure.

Rectification of the register of members may be available under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 where its requirements are met; assess whether the dispute belongs before the NCLT and whether other remedies apply.
NCLT Rules, 2016 for procedure and forms.

Obtain a certified record of the company: MCA filings (publicly available records), financial statements, charges and director changes, and the register of members. Check eligibility to apply under Section 244.
Make a written request to the company for accounts and records, with copies of notices and minutes.
Map the conduct: dates of meetings, notices, resolutions, related-party transactions, dividend history and compensation of family members.
Assess whether a negotiated exit is feasible. Where it is, require an independent valuation basis.

If proceeding, prepare a petition before the Tribunal with a clear chronology, the legal grounds and specific reliefs (for example, buy-out at fair value, restoration of rights, restraint on transactions) and an interim application if assets are at risk.
Anticipate defences: majority rule, business judgment, delay, lack of standing.

docs.x: Share certificates and transfer records; MCA records; financial statements; board and general meeting notices and minutes; correspondence; bank statements if lawfully available; evidence of related-party dealings.

forum.x: National Company Law Tribunal bench with territorial jurisdiction over the registered office; appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal.

items: If oppression is established, the Tribunal may order a buy-out at fair value, regulate future conduct or set aside specific transactions.
If the conduct reflects ordinary commercial decisions within the majority's powers, relief may be refused.
Delay and weak evidence can weaken the case.

lessons.x: "Being outvoted is oppression." It is not by itself. "I can wait until the company recovers." Delay can hurt. Keep records and request information in writing.

faq: Do I need a minimum shareholding to apply?
The Act sets thresholds but the Tribunal can waive them in appropriate cases.
Can I get paid out?
A buy-out is one remedy the Tribunal can order if grounds are made out.

notcovered.x: Listed companies, class actions, fraud investigations by the government, foreign shareholders.

sources.x: Companies Act 2013 and rules; NCLT Rules 2016; MCA portal; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: GST Show-Cause Notice and Appeal
scenarios.meta_title: GST Show-Cause Notice and Appeal | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on responding to a GST show-cause notice over input tax credit and appealing the order in India, including Section 74A and...
scenarios.question: How to respond to a GST show-cause notice and appeal an order.

facts.x: A fictional trading company receives a show-cause notice alleging it wrongly claimed input tax credit because certain suppliers did not pay tax to the government or did not file returns. The notice covers periods in two financial years: one in FY 2023-24 and one in FY 2024-25. The precise tax periods and alleged conduct must be separated before choosing the statutory provision. The company paid its suppliers by bank transfer and holds tax invoices.

problem.x: Responding to the notice on time, choosing the right legal provision, and preserving appeal rights, including any pre-deposit.

items: Which section the notice should invoke for each period.
Eligibility conditions for input tax credit and the effect of a supplier's default.
Whether the department alleges fraud or suppression.
Time limits for the notice and order.
Appeal and pre-deposit.

CGST Act, 2017: Sections 73 and 74 generally address determination for periods up to FY 2023-24 (non-fraud and fraud/wilful-misstatement/suppression cases respectively); Section 74A generally applies to determination for FY 2024-25 onwards. Verify the exact period, applicable amendments, notice and order limitation, and statutory exceptions against the current Act and notifications. Do not imply that the supplier's default alone automatically resolves entitlement to ITC.

CGST Act Section 16 sets conditions for input tax credit, including possession of prescribed documents, receipt of goods/services, supplier-related conditions, return filing and time limits, as amended. Sections 16(5) and 16(6) introduced retrospective/relief provisions for specified periods and circumstances; assess their exact scope and any relevant circulars for the taxpayer.

Appeal to the Appellate Authority under Section 107: the ordinary limitation period and condonable extension are statutory and run from communication of the order. A pre-deposit is generally required. The amount, caps, and special rules for penalty-only orders must be calculated from the currently effective amended Sections 107 and 112 and applicable commencement notifications; do not rely on an unverified date or generic percentage.

Appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under Section 112 is subject to separate limitation and pre-deposit requirements. Confirm the relevant Tribunal's operational status, notified benches, filing rules and any transitional directions at the time of filing.
State GST Acts, which mirror the central provisions.
Writ jurisdiction of the High Court in limited circumstances such as lack of jurisdiction or breach of natural justice.
Read the notice: period, provision invoked, quantum, alleged ground, and the response deadline.
Check whether the provision matches the period (73 or 74 for earlier years; 74A for FY 2024-25 onwards) and whether time limits for the notice are met.
Collect proof of bona fides: invoices, e-way bills, transport records, bank payment proof, GSTR-2B reconciliations, and supplier registration status at the time.
File a reasoned reply on the statutory portal within the stated time, request a personal hearing and attach documents.
If an adverse order follows, calendar the appeal deadline from the date of communication. Check the pre-deposit, and file with the required deposit.
Consider writ remedies only where the circumstances justify bypassing the statutory appeal.
Review internal compliance: supplier due diligence, reconciliation routines and invoice matching.

docs.x: Show-cause notice and order; invoices and e-way bills; payment proofs; transport and delivery records; return filings and reconciliations; supplier registration and filing status.

forum.x: Adjudicating authority; Appellate Authority; Appellate Tribunal; High Court where appropriate.

items: Strong documentary proof of genuine transactions can help, though courts and authorities apply the statutory conditions strictly.
A procedural defect in the notice or order may result in setting aside or remand.
Pre-deposit is generally a condition for appeal, so cash-flow planning matters.

lessons.x: "The old section numbers always apply." Later periods fall under Section 74A. "Appeal deadlines are flexible." The Act allows only a limited condonation. Missing the reply or appeal date is usually more damaging than the underlying tax issue.

faq: Do I have to pay anything to appeal?
Generally a percentage of the disputed amount as pre-deposit, plus any admitted amount; check current rules.
Can I lose credit because my supplier did not pay tax?

ITC depends on the statutory conditions and the applicable period. The effect of a supplier's default is fact-sensitive and should be assessed against the Act, rules, circulars and binding case law; payment to a supplier and possession of an invoice do not by themselves guarantee credit.

notcovered.x: Refund claims, classification disputes, anti-profiteering, customs.

sources.x: CGST Act 2017 and Rules; State GST Acts; CBIC notifications and circulars; GST portal; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: Operational Creditor Insolvency Application
scenarios.meta_title: Operational Creditor Insolvency Application | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on an operational creditor's insolvency application against a company in India: demand notice, disputes, thresholds and recent IBC...
scenarios.question: When can a supplier or service provider start insolvency proceedings, and what are the risks?

facts.x: A fictional service provider ("the Creditor") has unpaid invoices from a fictional company ("the Company"). The Company has stopped responding, says some invoices relate to disputed work, and has not paid the undisputed part. The Creditor is considering an insolvency application.

problem.x: Whether insolvency is the right tool, what must be shown, and what the Company can do in response.

items: Whether the debt is an operational debt and above the minimum default threshold.
Whether there is a genuine pre-existing dispute.
The statutory demand notice and the response period.
Limitation.
Consequences of admission and the risk of misuse.
The effect of the 2026 amendments.

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC): an operational creditor ordinarily serves a demand notice under Section 8 and may apply under Section 9 after the statutory period if the requirements are met and no qualifying pre-existing dispute is shown. Admission can trigger a collective insolvency process and moratorium. Verify the current consolidated Code, rules and commencement notifications.

Minimum default threshold: verify the currently operative notification and any category-specific rule on the date of filing. Do not assume the original statutory amount remains the applicable threshold.
Limitation for applications under the Code and the extension of limitation by acknowledgment.
Distinguish enactment from commencement. If not verifiable from an official source, remove this detail from public-facing copy.

Information-utility requirements: verify whether any proposed or enacted requirement applies to this category of creditor and whether it is in force; do not describe a proposal as a current filing prerequisite.
Other routes: civil suit, summary suit, statutory routes for micro and small enterprises.
Establish that the debt is operational, due, above the threshold and within limitation. Gather invoices, delivery proof, and any acknowledgment.
Assess the dispute risk honestly. A real dispute raised before the demand notice is a common reason for rejection.
Consider alternatives: negotiated settlement, civil recovery, statutory remedies. Insolvency has far-reaching consequences and should not be used as ordinary pressure.
If proceeding, serve the statutory demand notice and observe the response period.
If no payment or dispute follows, prepare the application with the required documents and evidence of default.

Debtor side: respond within the statutory period, identify any genuine pre-existing dispute with contemporaneous evidence, consider settlement, and verify the currently effective withdrawal rules before taking a position.

docs.x: Contract and invoices; delivery or performance proof; ledger statements; demand notice and proof of delivery; the Company's replies; bank statements; any prior correspondence on the alleged dispute.

forum.x: National Company Law Tribunal; appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal; resolution professional and committee of creditors after admission.

items: Admission is more likely where default is clear and no genuine dispute pre-dates the demand notice.
Rejection is likely where a substantial pre-existing dispute is shown.
Settlement before admission is common.
Frivolous or abusive filings can attract costs or penalties.

lessons.x: "Insolvency is a fast way to get paid." It is a collective process, not an individual recovery tool. "Any unpaid bill qualifies." Thresholds and conditions apply. Record disputes in writing as they arise.

faq: Can I withdraw after filing?

Withdrawal is governed by the IBC, applicable regulations and judicial orders, and the position may differ before and after constitution of the committee of creditors. Check the current text and applicable approval requirements.
What if the other side says the work was defective?
A genuine, documented dispute can prevent admission.

notcovered.x: Financial creditor applications, personal insolvency, cross-border insolvency, liquidation.

sources.x: IBC 2016 as amended, including the 2026 Act; IBBI regulations; NCLT rules; commencement notifications; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: SARFAESI Enforcement Against a Borrower
scenarios.meta_title: SARFAESI Enforcement Against a Borrower | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on challenging SARFAESI enforcement of a mortgaged property in India: demand notice, possession, the Debt Recovery Tribunal and...
scenarios.question: How can a borrower challenge a bank's enforcement against mortgaged property?

facts.x: A fictional borrower's term loan, secured by a mortgage over a commercial property, becomes a non-performing asset. The lender issues a demand notice, the borrower sends a representation and proposes a one-time settlement, the lender communicates its response, and possession is then taken with assistance from the District Magistrate. Whether the response and possession comply with law depends on the documents and the applicable procedure. A sale notice follows.

problem.x: Protecting the property from sale, testing the lender's compliance, and exploring settlement or restructuring.

items: Whether the loan was properly classified and the notice properly issued.
Whether the lender considered the borrower's representation and gave reasons.
Compliance in taking possession and in conducting the sale.
The remedy before the Tribunal and its time limit.
Pre-deposit for further appeal.
Right to redeem.

SARFAESI Act, 2002: Section 13(2) generally requires a 60-day demand notice; Section 13(3A) addresses consideration of the borrower's representation and communication of reasons; Section 13(4) lists enforcement measures; Section 14 concerns assistance by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate/District Magistrate; Section 17 provides an application to the DRT ordinarily within 45 days of the measure challenged; Section 18 governs appeal to the DRAT and generally requires a deposit of 50% of the debt due, reducible by the DRAT for recorded reasons to not less than 25%. Verify the current text and facts.
Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993: procedure before the Tribunal.
Exclusions and limits on the Act's application, such as certain securities and smaller dues.
Interaction with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: a moratorium in insolvency can restrain enforcement.
Obtain the loan documents, notice, classification letters and all enforcement notices; note receipt dates.
Check whether the notice period, representation process and reasons requirement were followed.
Calendar the Tribunal application deadline from the date of the enforcement measure and prepare the application with grounds, prayer for interim protection and a statement of dues.
Explore settlement or restructuring in parallel, including a one-time settlement, with a written, approved proposal.
Be ready to pay or deposit amounts the Tribunal may require as a condition of interim protection.
Track the sale process urgently.
If the Tribunal's order is adverse, assess appeal and the pre-deposit.

docs.x: Loan agreement and security documents; account statements; classification notice; demand notice and representation; lender's reply; possession and sale notices; valuation reports; settlement correspondence.

forum.x: Debt Recovery Tribunal; Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal; High Court under Article 226 in narrow circumstances.

items: Procedural non-compliance can invalidate a step and lead to relief.
Tribunals often condition interim protection on a deposit.
A negotiated settlement is a common resolution.

lessons.x: "A representation stops the lender." It does not by itself; the lender must consider it. "I can challenge whenever I like." The period to approach the Tribunal is short. Keep every notice and its date of receipt.

faq: How long do I have to challenge enforcement?

A Section 17 application is ordinarily required within 45 days of the relevant measure under Section 13(4). Identify the exact measure and calculate limitation immediately; do not assume that a representation or settlement discussion stops time.
Can the sale be stopped?
Interim protection depends on the facts, statutory compliance and the Tribunal's or court's order. Filing a challenge does not automatically stay the sale.

notcovered.x: Agricultural land and other excluded security, guarantor-specific issues, asset reconstruction company assignments.

sources.x: SARFAESI Act 2002 and Rules; RDB Act 1993; RBI circulars on classification and settlement; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: Defective Product Consumer Complaint
scenarios.meta_title: Defective Product Consumer Complaint | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a consumer complaint for a defective appliance in India: which Commission, limitation, evidence and mediation.
scenarios.question: How to file a consumer complaint for defective goods or deficient service.

facts.x: A fictional consumer buys an appliance with a one-year warranty from a retailer. It fails within months. The retailer redirects to the manufacturer's service centre. The service centre cancels visits and gives no repair date. Written complaints go unanswered.

problem.x: Getting a repair, replacement or refund, plus compensation for the inconvenience, with minimal cost.

items: Whether the buyer is a "consumer" for the purchase.
Defect in goods and deficiency in service.
Which parties to name.
Which Commission has jurisdiction by value and by territory.
Limitation.
Evidence.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019: consider the definitions of consumer, defect, deficiency and unfair trade practice; applicable remedies and product-liability provisions; mediation provisions; and the two-year limitation period from the cause of action, subject to the Commission's power to condone delay for sufficient cause. Check the precise statutory section and facts.
Pecuniary jurisdiction by value of consideration paid, per the 2021 Rules: District up to Rs 50 lakh; State above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore; National above Rs 2 crore.

Territorial jurisdiction may include the place where the complainant resides or personally works for gain, subject to the Consumer Protection Act and the facts. Check the current statutory wording and whether the complaint is maintainable against each opposite party.
Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 where the product was bought online.
Confirm the currently operational electronic filing portal, applicable filing procedure, court fee and rules before advising; portal names and processes may change.
Gather invoice, warranty terms, photos or videos of the defect, service tickets and all complaints.
Send a clear written notice to the seller and manufacturer stating the defect, the relief sought and a reasonable deadline.
Consider mediation, which the Act supports where parties agree.
If unresolved, prepare a complaint to the right Commission, with facts, documents, relief and a statement on limitation.
Seek a technical or service report if the defect is technical and disputed.
After an order, follow the enforcement provisions if there is non-compliance.

docs.x: Invoice; warranty card; product details; defect evidence; service history; written complaints with proof of delivery; correspondence; any payment evidence.

forum.x: The District Commission is ordinarily the first-instance forum for claims within its current pecuniary jurisdiction. State and National Commission jurisdiction depends on the Act and Rules; appellate routes and deposit requirements must be separately checked. The illustrative facts do not specify a purchase value, so do not assert a forum until that value is supplied.

items: Where defect and non-redress are shown, Commissions may order repair, replacement or refund with compensation and costs.
Missing documents or delay can weaken the case.
Settlement during proceedings is common.

lessons.x: "Only the manufacturer is responsible." The seller can also be liable. "No deadline applies." The limitation period is two years, with limited condonation. Keep every document and message.

faq: Do I need a lawyer?
Parties may represent themselves, though legal advice can help with drafting and evidence.
Which Commission?

Pecuniary jurisdiction is based on the value of consideration paid for the goods or services, not simply the compensation demanded. Territorial jurisdiction is a separate test. Confirm the current limits and the complainant's facts.

notcovered.x: Product liability class actions, housing and builder disputes, insurance claims.

sources.x: Consumer Protection Act 2019; 2020 and 2021 Rules; consumer affairs ministry notifications; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: Data Protection Readiness for a Retailer
scenarios.meta_title: Data Protection Readiness for a Retailer | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on preparing an online business for India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and Rules: phased dates, notices, consent, rights...
scenarios.question: What must a business do under India's data protection law and when?

facts.x: A fictional online retailer collects names, contacts, addresses and purchase histories, and has started using these for marketing messages without a clear notice. A customer asks the retailer to delete their data. The retailer uses third-party vendors for payments and delivery and stores data on cloud servers.

problem.x: What legal obligations apply now, what will apply later, and how to prepare without overpromising compliance.

items: Which law governs today and which obligations are not yet in force.
Notice and consent for marketing.
Handling the customer's deletion request.
Vendor contracts.
Security and breach readiness.
Penalties and governance.

Until the relevant DPDP provisions commence, other applicable laws and rules may continue to govern relevant processing, including the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the SPDI Rules, 2011 to the extent applicable. Check the DPDP Act's repeal/amendment and commencement provisions, the type of data and processing, and sector-specific obligations; do not assume every pre-existing rule applies to every dataset.
Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, which may apply independently.

The Act and Rules address notice, consent, certain legitimate uses, data-principal rights, security safeguards, personal-data-breach notifications, children's data and additional obligations for Significant Data Fiduciaries. The exact duty, exceptions, timelines and commencement date differ by provision; confirm each from the official text before describing it as currently mandatory.
Penalties under the Act's schedule; the exact amounts and conditions must be read from the Act and not summarised without verification.
Map data: what is collected, why, where it is stored, who receives it and how long it is kept.
Identify which obligations apply today and which will apply from the later commencement dates; build a dated plan.
Revise the privacy notice to describe actual processing; separate marketing consent from order fulfilment.
Create a process for customer requests (access, correction, deletion) with a log and response timelines to be confirmed once the relevant provisions commence.
Review vendor contracts for security, sub-processing, breach cooperation and deletion.
Prepare an incident response plan and internal training.
Review children's data practices if any users may be minors.

docs.x: Data inventory; current privacy notice and consent screens; vendor agreements; security policies; retention schedule; incident log; customer request records.

forum.x: Compliance is primarily internal and regulatory. The Act establishes the Data Protection Board of India; confirm its constitution, operational status, applicable rules and the commencement of the relevant powers before stating which complaints it can currently receive or decide.

items: A business that maps data, updates notices and tightens vendor contracts will be better placed when obligations commence.
Marketing based on data collected for another purpose is a common compliance gap.
Compliance timelines can change through further notifications.

lessons.x: "The law is not in force, so I can wait." Some provisions are in force and others commence in stages; preparation takes time. "A policy page is enough." The notice must match actual processing.

faq: Can a customer demand deletion today under the new Act?

The answer depends on the exact commencement status and any other applicable law, contract or sectoral rule. Check the official enforcement timeline and the facts; do not categorically deny or promise a deletion right.
Does the law apply to small businesses?
Size alone should not be treated as a blanket exemption. Applicability and any exemption depend on the Act, Rules, processing and current commencement status.

notcovered.x: Cross-border transfers beyond a general mention, significant data fiduciary audits, sector-specific rules for banking, health, telecom.

sources.x: DPDP Act 2023; DPDP Rules 2025; Gazette commencement notifications; MeitY website; IT Act 2000 and rules; E-Commerce Rules 2020.

scenarios.title: Cartel Investigation by the CCI
scenarios.meta_title: Cartel Investigation by the CCI | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a competition investigation into price information exchange and refusal to supply: presumption, leniency, penalties on global...
scenarios.question: What are the risks and options when a competition regulator investigates a suspected cartel?

facts.x: Three fictional regional distributors of an industrial product exchanged messages about upcoming prices and agreed not to supply a new entrant. A trade body staff member heard of this and a complaint followed. The Competition Commission of India ("CCI") has sent a notice seeking information. The scenario assumes a valid notice; the recipient should check its scope, statutory basis, deadline and any available procedural objections.

problem.x: Each distributor must decide how to respond, whether to cooperate with the regulator, and how to limit exposure, while preserving privilege and avoiding obstruction.

items: Whether the conduct is a horizontal agreement presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition.
Evidence of the agreement and of its implementation.
Leniency.
Penalty calculation.
Settlement and commitment, and their limits.
Search and seizure and privilege.
Appeal.

Competition Act, 2002, Section 3 (anti-competitive agreements; the presumption for certain horizontal agreements, including price fixing, limiting supply and market allocation; and rule-of-reason analysis for other agreements).

Sections 19 and 26 (inquiry, prima facie opinion, investigation by the Director General); Section 27 (orders, including penalties); Section 41 (Director General's powers, including search and seizure).
Section 46 and the leniency regulations: reduced penalty for first-in cartel participants who make full and true disclosure; the 2023 amendments added "leniency plus".
Penalties: the Amendment Act provides for penalties calculated on global turnover; the CCI's penalty guidelines and turnover regulations govern the method.
Appeals to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Section 53B).

Privilege and confidentiality in competition investigations: verify the applicable statutory provisions and current authority, including whether the communication and the lawyer's role qualify for protection. Do not assume that all in-house legal communications are privileged.
Issue a document preservation notice. Do not delete or alter records.
Engage competition counsel and, separately, consider whether conflicts require separate representation of individuals and the company.
Conduct a privileged internal review of communications to understand the facts.
Evaluate leniency promptly; position in the queue can matter.
Respond to the information request accurately and on time, with careful scope.
Prepare for a possible Director General investigation and for the penalty stage; review financial information relevant to turnover.
Implement a compliance programme and training regardless of outcome.

docs.x: Notice from the CCI; trade body communications; messages and emails among competitors; pricing and supply records; refusal-to-supply correspondence; turnover and financial statements; any compliance policies.

forum.x: Competition Commission of India; Director General; National Company Law Appellate Tribunal; Supreme Court.

items: If the exchange and the boycott are established, penalties can be significant and are now assessed with reference to turnover as defined in the amended law.

A qualifying applicant may be considered for a reduction under the operative leniency framework; eligibility, order of priority and disclosure requirements must be checked against current regulations.
Weak evidence of an agreement may lead to closure.

lessons.x: "Sharing prices informally is harmless." It can be treated as a cartel facilitator. "We can fix this later." Leniency and cooperation depend on timing. Preserve documents; never destroy records once an inquiry is anticipated.

faq: Are penalties based only on Indian sales?
The 2023 amendments introduced a global turnover basis; confirm the current method.

notcovered.x: Abuse of dominance, merger filings, sector regulators.

sources.x: Competition Act 2002 and the 2023 Amendment Act; CCI regulations and guidelines; commencement notifications; official repository for authority.

scenarios.title: Pollution Control Board Notice to a Factory
scenarios.meta_title: Pollution Control Board Notice to a Factory | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a State pollution control board notice, consent renewal, closure directions, penalties and appeals to the National Green...
scenarios.question: What can a factory do when a pollution control board issues a notice or directions?

facts.x: A fictional manufacturing unit holds consent to operate that is due for renewal. After a complaint from neighbours, the State pollution control board inspects, finds exceedances in stack emissions and effluent, issues a show-cause notice and directs a corrective plan within a period, warning of closure.

problem.x: Keeping the unit lawfully operating, responding credibly, and understanding which proceedings can lead to penalties or closure.

items: The legal basis of the board's notice and directions.
Compliance with consent conditions.
Renewal and any deemed-consent rule.
Penalties and the adjudication process after the 2023-2024 amendments.
Appeals.
Whether criminal liability remains for some contraventions.

Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, as amended by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023: consent (Section 21), directions (Section 31A), and monetary penalties through adjudication.
Rules on holding inquiry and imposing penalty issued in November 2024.
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: general directions and penalties, as amended.

National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: the NGT has only the jurisdiction and appellate powers conferred by statute. Identify the exact provision permitting an appeal from the particular order; do not imply that every board notice, direction or adjudication order is appealable to the NGT.

Do not assume deemed consent from delay. Check whether a deemed-consent provision applies to the relevant State, category of industry, statute and application, and whether all statutory prerequisites were met.
Identify the legal basis of each notice and the stated deadline.
Commission an independent environmental audit of emissions and effluent against consent conditions and standards.
Submit a considered reply with the audit findings and a time-bound corrective action plan, including installation or repair of control equipment.
File the renewal application in time with complete documents; keep proof of filing for any deemed-consent argument.
If the board issues a closure or stoppage direction, assess immediate appeal and interim relief.
Track adjudication proceedings for penalties and the appeal route with deposit.
Set up a compliance calendar and monitoring records.

docs.x: Consent orders and conditions; inspection reports; monitoring data; board notices and replies; audit report; equipment records; renewal application and proof of filing.

forum.x: State Pollution Control Board; adjudicating officer; National Green Tribunal; High Court under Article 226 in narrow cases.

items: A credible corrective plan and verified data may be relevant to the regulator's response, but do not guarantee that closure or other directions will be avoided.
Penalties are monetary for many contraventions; continued non-compliance can escalate.
Where operating without valid consent is alleged, the consequences may be more serious.

lessons.x: "Renewal can wait." Missing the renewal window risks operating without valid consent. Keep monitoring data.

faq: Can the board shut my unit?
It can issue directions within its statutory powers, which can be challenged through the appeal routes.
Where do I appeal a penalty?
Generally to the National Green Tribunal, with a deposit; confirm current rules.

notcovered.x: Environmental impact assessment clearances, waste management rules, forest clearance, mining.

sources.x: Water Act 1974 as amended; Air Act 1981 as amended; Jan Vishwas Act 2023; Environment (Protection) Act 1986; NGT Act 2010; board consent conditions; official repository.

scenarios.title: Fire Insurance Claim Repudiation
scenarios.meta_title: Fire Insurance Claim Repudiation | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on an insurer rejecting a business fire claim for alleged non-disclosure in India: duty of disclosure, surveyor reports, remedies...
scenarios.question: Can an insurer reject a claim for non-disclosure, and what can the policyholder do?

facts.x: A fictional small business has a fire policy over its premises and stock. After a fire, a surveyor assesses the loss. The insurer repudiates the claim, alleging that the business did not disclose an earlier minor fire loss on the proposal form. The business says the earlier incident was disclosed to the agent orally.

problem.x: Recovering the loss and testing whether the repudiation is legally sound.

items: Duty of disclosure and materiality.
Whether the insurer proved non-disclosure and its materiality.
The role and report of the surveyor.
The policy terms and any time limits in the policy.
The correct forum: consumer, civil or arbitration.
The effect of the 2025 amendments.
Duty of utmost good faith and disclosure of material facts in insurance contracts; Indian Contract Act, 1872 provisions on misrepresentation and fraud; policy terms and proposal form.
Insurance Act, 1938. The statutory rule that limits repudiation after a stated period (Section 45) is framed for life insurance; do not assume it applies to a fire policy.

Surveyors and loss assessors are governed by the Insurance Act and applicable IRDAI regulations. Verify the currently operative policyholder-protection and claims regulations, their timelines, exceptions and the legal weight of the survey report. Do not imply that the surveyor's assessment automatically binds the insurer or court.
Insurance Ombudsman eligibility, subject-matter jurisdiction, monetary limits, exclusions, prior representation requirements and limitation must be checked under the rules in force.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019: maintainability must be assessed under the Act and binding case law. Do not assume that a business insurance policy either automatically qualifies or automatically fails the consumer test; analyse the insured, purpose, policy and relief sought.
Arbitration clauses in policies and limitation clauses; Limitation Act, 1963 for a suit.
Obtain the policy, proposal form, survey report and the repudiation letter with its reasons.
Reconstruct what was disclosed, to whom and when. Gather evidence of the oral disclosure and the agent's role.
Test materiality: would the earlier loss have affected the insurer's decision to insure or the terms?
Write a detailed representation to the insurer's grievance process, attaching evidence.
Choose the forum with care: civil suit, consumer complaint (if maintainable), arbitration under the policy, or the ombudsman if eligible.
Quantify the loss with documents: accounts, stock records, invoices, repair estimates.
Watch limitation and any policy time limits.

docs.x: Policy and endorsements; proposal form; agent communications; surveyor report; claim form and supporting accounts; repudiation letter; fire brigade or police report; loss evidence.

forum.x: Insurer's grievance cell; Insurance Ombudsman if eligible; civil court; consumer commission if maintainable; arbitrator if the policy requires.

items: If the insurer fails to prove materiality or the policyholder shows disclosure, the repudiation may be set aside.
If material non-disclosure is established, the claim can fail.
A negotiated or partial settlement may be possible, depending on the policy, evidence, insurer and applicable procedure; it is not an assumed or typical outcome.

lessons.x: "Insurers cannot repudiate after taking premium." They can in some circumstances. "Telling the agent is always enough." It depends on the facts and the agent's role. Read the proposal form carefully and keep copies.

faq: Does the three-year rule on challenging policies apply to fire cover?
That rule is framed for life insurance; check the Act before relying on it.
Where do I complain?
It depends on the type of policy and policyholder; there may be several routes.

notcovered.x: Life and health insurance claims, motor claims, marine cargo, reinsurance.

sources.x: Insurance Act 1938 as amended in 2025; IRDAI regulations; Contract Act 1872; Consumer Protection Act 2019; Insurance Ombudsman rules; official repository.

scenarios.title: School Admission Cancelled After Fees
scenarios.meta_title: School Admission Cancelled After Fees | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a private school cancelling an admission and retaining fees in India: fee regulation, refund, grievance routes and possible forums.
scenarios.question: What can parents do when a private school cancels an admission and keeps fees?

facts.x: A fictional private school confirms a child's admission, collects the first instalment and an admission fee, then cancels it citing an incomplete document. The family says it submitted the document by email and in person. The school refuses to refund the fee.

problem.x: Restoring the admission or recovering the amount paid, without harming the child's schooling.

items: The terms of admission and fee policy.
Whether the school followed its own procedure.
Whether State fee regulation or refund rules apply.
Whether the school's acts are open to challenge in a writ court or only in civil or consumer forums.
Evidence of submission.

The prospectus, admission form, fee policy and communications are relevant evidence of the terms, but do not assume they alone determine the dispute; mandatory State law, statutory rules, public policy and consumer-law maintainability may affect the result.
State education legislation and fee regulation, if any, for private schools in the relevant State (for example, State laws on fee regulation of self-financed schools).
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, to the extent relevant to the school type and class.
Consumer Protection Act, 2019: courts and commissions have addressed whether educational institutions' services fall within "service"; the answer has depended on the nature of the service and claim.

Article 226: maintainability against a private unaided school is fact- and duty-specific. A public function alone should not be treated as an automatic answer; identify the enforceable public/statutory duty and verify the controlling Supreme Court and High Court authority.
Any regulator or State fee-refund guideline must be identified by name, legal authority, institution type, level of education and current applicability.
Collect proof of submission: email with attachments, sent items, courier receipts, acknowledgments.
Write to the school stating the facts and asking for reasons and reconsideration or a full refund.
Use the State grievance machinery, such as a district education officer or fee regulatory committee if it exists.
Consider mediation or a legal notice.
Evaluate forums: civil suit for refund, consumer complaint if maintainable, or writ if a statutory duty is involved.
Protect the child: seek alternative admission in parallel if timelines matter.

docs.x: Admission letter; fee receipts; prospectus and policies; proof of document submission; school's cancellation letter and reasons; emails and messages.

forum.x: State education authority; civil court; consumer commission if maintainable; High Court under Article 226 where justified.

items: Where the school did not follow its own policy or the State's fee rules, refund or reinstatement may be ordered or negotiated.
Where the contract allows forfeiture and the school followed it, recovery can be limited.

lessons.x: "Schools can keep any fee." State rules and the contract matter. "A writ lies against every school." It depends on the school's character and duty. Keep dated proof of every submission.

faq: Can a private school keep admission fees?
It depends on the terms and any State regulation.
Should I go to court or the education department?
The appropriate route depends on the governing State law, urgency, available statutory remedy and limitation; a grievance representation does not necessarily stop limitation.

notcovered.x: Higher education regulators, exam disputes, scholarships, minority institutions.

sources.x: Applicable State education and fee laws; RTE Act 2009; Contract Act 1872; Consumer Protection Act 2019; official repository.

scenarios.title: AI Voice Clone in an Advertisement
scenarios.meta_title: AI Voice Clone in an Advertisement | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on an unauthorised AI-generated voice in an advertisement in India: personality rights, passing off, performers' rights, platform...
scenarios.question: What rights does a performer have against an AI voice clone used in advertising?

facts.x: A fictional voice performer finds an advertisement featuring a voice that sounds like theirs, produced by an AI tool, endorsing a product they have never worked with. The ad is running on social media and a streaming platform.

problem.x: Stopping the use quickly, identifying the responsible parties and seeking compensation.

items: Whether personality or publicity rights protect the voice and persona.
Passing off and false endorsement.
Performers' rights and moral rights under copyright law.
Advertising and consumer law.
Intermediary takedown.
Evidence and attribution.
Interim relief against unknown persons.

Personality and publicity rights as developed by High Courts through injunctions in cases involving public figures and misuse of name, image and voice; the scope for non-celebrity performers is less clear.
Passing off and false endorsement as part of common law.

Copyright Act, 1957: confirm the precise performer-right and moral-right provisions, ownership and duration. Training on or imitating a recording does not by itself resolve infringement; identify the protected subject matter and the relevant act, licence and evidence.

Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, as currently amended: verify the exact intermediary duty, notice/takedown route, deadlines and any operative synthetic-content requirements. Distinguish notified rules from draft amendments or consultation proposals.
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and guidelines on misleading advertisements and endorsements; liability of endorsers and advertisers.
Penal provisions on cheating by personation or identity theft online.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025: a voice recording may be personal data where it relates to an identifiable individual, but applicability depends on the processing and statutory definitions/exemptions. Check the official phased commencement timeline; do not say that all obligations are or are not in force without checking the specific provision.
Preserve evidence: screenshots, URLs, recordings, timestamps, and a comparison with genuine recordings.
Identify the advertiser, agency and platforms. Send notices to platforms using their grievance channels and the legal takedown routes.
Send a cease-and-desist to the advertiser and agency, demanding withdrawal, disclosure of the tool and source data, and an account.
Consider an urgent suit for injunction, including orders against unknown persons where the court allows, and orders directed to intermediaries.
Assess damages and an account of profits.
Prevent recurrence: licensing terms for voice data, contract clauses on AI use, and watch monitoring.

docs.x: Evidence of the advertisement; genuine recordings and contracts; proof of reputation and earnings; takedown correspondence; platform responses; advertiser details.

forum.x: High Court or the civil or commercial court with jurisdiction; platform grievance officers; advertising self-regulation bodies; consumer protection authority for misleading advertisements.

items: Interim relief may be available on the facts, but the scope of personality rights, especially for non-celebrities and AI-generated imitations, remains fact-sensitive and must be supported by current authority.
Platforms may remove content on valid notice.
Damages depend on proof of loss and of use.

lessons.x: "There is no law against AI voice clones." Several legal bases may apply, though the law is developing. "Takedown solves everything." It does not compensate. Keep clear contracts on voice use.

faq: Does a voice have legal protection?
It can be protected through several routes, depending on the facts.
Can the platform be forced to remove the ad?
It can be asked, and courts can direct intermediaries in appropriate cases.

notcovered.x: Deepfake sexual content, political deepfakes, training-data copyright claims.

sources.x: Copyright Act 1957; IT Act 2000 and the 2021 Rules as amended; Consumer Protection Act 2019; official repository for personality-rights authority.

scenarios.title: Charitable Trust Dispute Among Trustees
scenarios.meta_title: Charitable Trust Dispute Among Trustees | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a dispute over charitable funds and a property transfer in an Indian trust: duties of trustees, State charity regulators, civil...
scenarios.question: What can be done about alleged breach of trust in a charitable trust?

facts.x: A fictional charitable trust runs a school. Two trustees allege that a third trustee, with a relative, arranged to sell a trust property below value and used donations for unrelated expenses. The trust deed requires majority approval for sale of property.

problem.x: Protecting trust assets, correcting any breach, and avoiding loss of tax registration.

items: Whether the trust is private or public and which statute governs it.
Compliance with the deed and approvals.
Duties of trustees and conflicts of interest.
Remedies: accounts, setting aside, removal, recovery.
Limitation.
Tax and registration consequences.
Indian Trusts Act, 1882 for private trusts and general principles of trusteeship: duties, accounts, breach of trust and removal.

For public charitable trusts, the position varies by State: some States have comprehensive public trusts or endowment statutes and charity commissioners; where none applies, Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 allows suits for breach of public charitable trust with leave of court.

Limitation Act, 1963: identify the exact article and nature of relief. Any special rule for suits against express trustees is narrow and should not be generalised to every claim involving a trust or its property.
If the body is a society or a Section 8 company, the Societies Registration Act, 1860 as applicable in the State, or the Companies Act, 2013.

Income-tax legislation and transitional provisions: identify the statute and provisions applicable to the relevant tax year, registration status, transaction and filing. Verify the Income-tax Act, 2025 and any savings/transitional rules against the official Act and commencement notifications; do not assume that the same Act governs all earlier and later years. review by a qualified tax adviser is mandatory.

Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, if foreign contribution is involved: verify registration/prior permission, permitted receipt and utilisation, bank-account, reporting and restriction requirements on current official sources.
Obtain the trust deed, registration documents, minutes, accounts and property records.
Identify the governing law and regulator.
Demand accounts and explanations; call a trustee meeting with proper notice and record resolutions.
Where appropriate, make a representation to the charity regulator or file the proceeding the State law provides.
If a suit is needed, seek interim orders restraining further alienation, and the remedies of accounts, recovery and removal.
Involve a tax qualified professional to assess registration risk and corrective filings.
Adopt a conflict-of-interest and approval policy.

docs.x: Trust deed; registration certificates; minutes; bank statements; sale documents and valuation; donation records; audit reports; tax filings.

forum.x: State charity commissioner or equivalent where it exists; civil court; High Court; tax authorities for registration issues.

items: Courts and regulators can restrain dealings with trust property, order accounts and, in serious cases, remove trustees.
A transaction below market value may be examined for breach of trust.

lessons.x: "All trusts are governed by the same law." Public and private trusts differ, and States differ. "Majority trustees can do as they wish." Duties and the deed constrain them.

faq: Can a trustee be removed?
Courts and regulators have power to remove trustees in appropriate cases under the governing law.
Is there a time limit?
Rules differ; some claims concerning trust property have special limitation rules.

notcovered.x: Religious endowments, waqf property, FCRA registration, charity tax structuring.

sources.x: Indian Trusts Act 1882; relevant State trust or charity law; CPC Section 92; Income-tax Act 2025 and 1961 Act for earlier years; FCRA 2010; official repository.

scenarios.title: Foreign Investment in an Indian Company
scenarios.meta_title: Foreign Investment in an Indian Company | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a foreign investor buying shares in an Indian private company: routes under FDI policy, land-border investor rules, pricing...
scenarios.question: What approvals, filings and structuring steps apply to a foreign investor buying into an Indian company?

facts.x: A fictional foreign fund wants to acquire a majority of the shares of a fictional Indian private company in a sector with foreign investment conditions. Some limited partners of the fund are in a country sharing a land border with India, holding small stakes.

problem.x: Confirming that the investment is permitted, the route (automatic or government approval), pricing rules, required filings and structuring risks.

items: Sectoral caps and conditions.
Land-border-country rules and beneficial ownership.
Pricing and valuation.
Reporting.
Competition law thresholds.
Tax consequences.
Foreign-law issues in the investor's own jurisdiction.

Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, with the Consolidated FDI Policy: permitted sectors, caps, automatic and approval routes, pricing guidelines and reporting.

Press Note 3 (2020 Series) and DPIIT Press Note 2 (2026 Series), together with any implementing FEMA notification: analyse the complete operative text and definitions of investor, beneficial owner, control, thresholds, sectoral conditions, reporting and prior approval.

Sector-specific FDI limits and routes change. Verify the current sectoral policy, applicable press note, FEMA rules/notification and conditions at signing and closing. Any insurance example must be checked against the operative policy and statutory commencement.
Companies Act, 2013 on share issue and transfer; Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules for private placements.
Competition Act, 2002: combination thresholds, including the deal value threshold.
Tax: capital gains, withholding, treaty and anti-avoidance issues; qualified professional review required.
Foreign law: the investor's home-law issues must be handled by qualified counsel in that jurisdiction. This practice would not advise on foreign law.
Define the structure: primary issuance, secondary purchase, instruments.
Verify sectoral cap and route. Map the fund's beneficial ownership against the land-border rules and the 10% non-controlling test.
Determine whether combination filing is needed.
Conduct due diligence and structure the transaction documents with conditions precedent for approvals.
Apply pricing and valuation requirements and obtain required valuation reports.
Complete the reporting filings after the transaction within the prescribed time.
Coordinate with tax advisers and foreign counsel.

docs.x: Fund structure chart and beneficial ownership details; shareholding of the target; sector classification; valuation reports; transaction documents; approvals; bank and remittance records.

forum.x: Reserve Bank of India and authorised dealer banks (reporting); the government approval route through the designated authority; Registrar of Companies; Competition Commission of India if applicable.

items: If the route is automatic and conditions are met, the transaction proceeds with reporting.
Where the operative policy requires prior Government approval, the transaction must not close on an assumption that approval can be obtained retrospectively.
Errors in route or pricing can lead to contraventions and compounding.

lessons.x: "Any small foreign stake is automatically fine." Beneficial ownership rules matter. "FDI rules are stable." They change often; verify at each step. Document the analysis.

faq: Do all foreign investments need government approval?
Many are under the automatic route, but sector and investor conditions can require approval.
Can an Indian advocate advise on the investor's home law?
No, that requires qualified counsel in that jurisdiction.

notcovered.x: Outward investment by Indian companies, portfolio investment in listed companies, external borrowings.

sources.x: FEMA 1999; NDI Rules 2019; Consolidated FDI Policy and press notes on the DPIIT website; RBI master directions; Companies Act 2013; Competition Act 2002.

scenarios.title: Legal Due Diligence in an Acquisition
scenarios.meta_title: Legal Due Diligence in an Acquisition | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on legal due diligence when buying a software company in India: IP ownership, open-source licences, employee claims, data, and...
scenarios.question: What does legal due diligence cover in a company acquisition and how do findings change the deal?

facts.x: A fictional buyer is acquiring all shares of a fictional software company. Diligence finds: a former employee has raised a claim for dues and wrongful termination; some code contains components under licences with source-code disclosure conditions; several developers were contractors with no written IP assignment; and privacy practices are informal.

problem.x: Understanding what the risks mean for price and terms, and how to protect the buyer through the agreement.

items: IP ownership and chain of title.
Open-source licence compliance.
Employment claims.
Data protection readiness.
Contractual and regulatory exposure.
How to allocate risk: price, indemnity, escrow, conditions.
Limits of legal diligence.

Copyright Act, 1957: verify first ownership under Section 17 and the applicable employment/commission exceptions; assignments must satisfy the Act's formalities, including Section 19 where applicable. Contractor-created code may remain with the contractor absent an effective assignment, but assess the actual contract, authorship, employment status, commissioned-work provisions and licence terms.

Open-source compliance depends on the specific licence, how the component is used/distributed and the code architecture. A licence does not invariably require disclosure of an entire proprietary codebase; obtain a software bill of materials and qualified technical and legal review.

Employment: verify commencement notifications, applicable rules and transitional provisions for each labour code and the worker's/employee's status. Assess contractual restrictions under current law, including the limits on post-termination restraints.

Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and Rules, 2025: commencement is phased. Check the official timeline for each relevant obligation at the transaction signing/closing date. Also assess the IT Act framework and other sectoral data/security requirements that remain applicable.
Companies Act, 2013 for share transfers; FEMA if the buyer is foreign; Competition Act thresholds.
Stamp duty on share transfer under the Indian Stamp Act as applicable.
Transaction documents: share purchase agreement, disclosure letter, warranties, indemnities, escrow, conditions precedent, covenants.
Agree scope and limits of the diligence, including that technical, tax and financial reviews need specialists.
Review corporate records, contracts, IP assignments, employment files, litigation and compliance.
Prepare a report with issues ranked by seriousness and with proposed actions.
Fix what can be fixed before signing: obtain confirmatory IP assignments from contractors, remediate licence issues, settle the employee claim.
Reflect remaining risks in the agreement: specific indemnities, price adjustment, escrow, conditions precedent and covenants.
Plan post-closing integration and compliance.
Maintain confidentiality in the data room.

docs.x: Constitutional documents and registers; contracts; IP registrations and assignments; code licence inventory; employment records; claim papers; privacy policies and vendor contracts; tax filings.

forum.x: Contractual and transactional; disputes under the agreement are handled under its dispute resolution clause.

items: Findings typically lead to a mix of remediation before closing and contractual protection.
Unresolved IP chain issues can affect value significantly.

lessons.x: "Due diligence guarantees there are no risks." It finds what the documents and disclosures reveal within the agreed scope. "Warranties alone are enough." Without remediation or specific indemnities, recovery can be hard. Do not skip contractor IP assignments.

faq: Who owns code written by contractors?
Often the contractor, unless there is a written assignment.
What happens to risks found in diligence?
They are addressed through price, indemnities, conditions or fixes.

notcovered.x: Cross-border carve-outs, listed company takeovers, tax structuring, technical code audits.

sources.x: Copyright Act 1957; Companies Act 2013; labour codes and rules; DPDP Act and Rules; FEMA rules; Competition Act 2002; official repository.

scenarios.title: RTI Request for Tender Records
scenarios.meta_title: RTI Request for Tender Records | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on a Right to Information request for public tender records in India: exemptions, personal information after the 2025 amendment...
scenarios.question: How does the Right to Information Act work now, and how can a refusal be challenged?

facts.x: A fictional unsuccessful bidder files an RTI request with a public authority for the evaluation sheet, the names of evaluation committee members and the winning bidder's technical bid. The Public Information Officer refuses, citing personal information and commercial confidence, without detailed reasons.

problem.x: Understanding what can be obtained, how to appeal, and how the recent amendment affects personal-information requests.

items: Exemptions for commercial confidence and personal information.
The effect of the amendment to the personal-information exemption.
Severability and partial disclosure.
The duty to give reasons.
Time limits for appeals.
Remedies if the Commission does not decide.

Right to Information Act, 2005: verify the current text of Sections 6, 7, 8, 10, 19 and 20, including response and appeal periods, as amended and commenced. Consider Section 11 third-party procedure where applicable. Do not promise disclosure of bid records: commercial confidence, third-party interests, public interest and severability require a record-specific analysis.
DPDP Act, 2023, Section 44(3): verify the official commencement notification and exact substituted text of RTI Act Section 8(1)(j).
State RTI rules and fee requirements.
Proactive disclosure duties of public authorities (Section 4) and tender transparency rules in procurement law.
Draft the request narrowly and specifically; ask for records, not opinions. Pay the fee as required.
Note the date of the request and the response deadline.
If refused, file the first appeal within the statutory period, arguing for partial disclosure and pointing to the absence of reasons.
If the first appeal fails or is not decided, file the second appeal to the Information Commission within its period.
Consider tender-specific remedies in parallel, such as a challenge to the award, through the proper forum.
If delay or non-compliance persists, consider remedies through the High Court.

docs.x: RTI application and proof of fee and delivery; refusal letter; first appeal and decision; tender notice and bid documents already available.

forum.x: Public Information Officer; first appellate authority; Central or State Information Commission; High Court under Article 226.

items: Disclosure of evaluation scores and award reasons depends on the records, applicable exemptions, third-party procedure and current authority; seek severable disclosure where appropriate.
Personal information may be withheld where the current statutory exemption applies; apply the amended text and binding authority rather than assuming a blanket rule.
Partial disclosure with redaction is a common result.

lessons.x: "RTI gives access to everything." Exemptions apply. Appeal deadlines are fixed; diary them.

faq: Can I get my competitor's bid?
Commercial secrets are protected, but some tender records may be disclosable.
Where do I appeal?
First to the appellate authority in the same public authority, then to the Information Commission.

notcovered.x: Information requests about private bodies, security and intelligence organisations, judicial records.

sources.x: RTI Act 2005 as amended; DPDP Act 2023 Section 44(3); State RTI rules; Commission decisions and official repository.

scenarios.title: Complaint About an Advocate's Conduct
scenarios.meta_title: Complaint About an Advocate's Conduct | Ink & Equity
scenarios.meta_desc: A hypothetical scenario on remedies for a client's complaint about an advocate in India: Bar Council disciplinary proceedings, civil claims and the...
scenarios.question: What remedies exist when a client is dissatisfied with an advocate?

facts.x: A fictional client engaged an advocate to file a case. Months later the client learns that the case was filed late, that an adverse interim order was passed and that the advocate did not tell them. The client wants to know the options.

problem.x: Understanding the difference between a disciplinary complaint and a damages claim, and the evidence needed.

items: What conduct can amount to professional misconduct.
The disciplinary procedure and its outcomes.
Civil liability for negligence.
Whether the Consumer Protection Act applies.
Fee and engagement issues.
Confidentiality and privilege.
Advocates Act, 1961: professional or other misconduct and the disciplinary jurisdiction of State Bar Councils (Section 35), the role of the Bar Council of India, and appeals.
Bar Council of India Rules on standards of professional conduct and etiquette, including duties to the client such as keeping the client informed.

Consumer law: the Supreme Court has held that advocates' professional services are not within the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 framework in Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Do not suggest a consumer complaint against an advocate as an available remedy unless later binding authority or legislation changes the position.

Civil remedies in contract or tort should be described cautiously: availability, standard of care, causation, limitation, proof of loss, privilege and public-policy issues require case-specific assessment. Do not imply that a civil damages claim necessarily lies merely because a client is dissatisfied.
Advocate-client privilege and confidentiality under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 and the Advocates Act.
Gather the engagement letter or instructions, fee receipts, case filings and dates, court orders and communications with the advocate.
Ask the advocate in writing for explanations and the file; consider a fresh advocate to protect the case and, where possible, rectify prejudice.
Decide whether to file a complaint with the State Bar Council, which may require a sworn statement and the prescribed form. Consider that disciplinary proceedings do not award compensation.
Assess a civil claim for damages and the burden of proving negligence and loss.
Do not assume a consumer forum is available.

docs.x: Engagement terms; payments; filings; orders; messages; evidence of loss.

forum.x: State Bar Council disciplinary committee; Bar Council of India on appeal; civil court for damages; High Court for related supervisory issues.

items: A disciplinary committee may impose only the sanctions authorised by the Advocates Act and applicable rules, after the prescribed process; verify the available sanction and appeal route.
A civil claim requires proof of duty, breach, causation and damage.
Mere error of judgment is not necessarily misconduct.

lessons.x: "A Bar Council will compensate me." It disciplines; it does not award damages. Keep a clear written record of instructions on both sides.

faq: Where do I complain about an advocate?
To the State Bar Council under the Advocates Act.
Can I get money back?
Through contract or civil claims, not through the disciplinary process alone.

notcovered.x: Complaints against judges, tribunal members or non-advocate legal service providers.

sources.x: Advocates Act 1961; Bar Council of India Rules; State Bar Council rules; the Supreme Court judgment and official repository; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023.
